newsitem.title: CHINA: HK parliament strikes down clutch of labour laws.
newsitem.headline: HK parliament strikes down clutch of labour laws.

text.p: Hong Kong's China-appointed parliament flexed its muscles in a fierce showdown with unions by striking down a clutch of labour rights laws late on Wednesday.

Clashing headlong with labour unions, members of the Provisional Legislative Council suspended four of seven laws which were enacted just before before China took back the 156-year-old British colony from London on July 1.
Legislators took the decision after a marathon debate, which they were forced to adjourn briefly when a small group of protesters stormed the public gallery of the chamber.
Three protesters brandished a huge red banner and shouted slogans before they were expelled after a brief struggle with security guards.
One of them, Leong Kwok-hung, accused the provisional legislature and the government of suppressing workers rights as he was dragged out of the building.
The issue is one of several disputes entangling post-colonial leader Tung Chee-hwa, his government and the unelected chamber.
The other quarrels are over his plan to harden up sedition laws, his bill to deport child illegal immigrants and an election law blueprint that would hamper pro-democracy forces.

Tung's government recommended that the seven laws should be suspended till the end of October to give it time to table counter-legislation. It argued that five of them would harm Hong Kong's economic competitiveness.
In an overall vote of 38 to nine with one abstention, legislators moved to suspend four of the seven laws, three dealing with labour rights and one with individual rights.
They involve such issues as the right of unions to bargain collectively with employers on wages and benefits on behalf of employees and the use of union funds for political activity.
The three laws to survive put limits on harbour reclamation, increase compensation for victims of occupational deafness and declare May 1 as a statutory holiday.
The debate and vote seemed certain to test the mettle of Hong Kong's embryonic free trade union movement.
Analysts said the new legislature might attack a whole raft of old legislation after rolling back one set of pre-handover laws passed by the disbanded, elected Legislative Council.

The decision also drew angry opposition from some legislators. "This administration attempts to undo all the lawful decisions that a former body decided. What messsge are we sending to the public? What confidence are we issuing to the public?" legislator Leong Che-hung asked within the chamber.
"I object to the way the administration attempts to pressurise this provisional legislature to pass bills in haste for the government's own administrative expedience," he added.
The three protesters who interrupted chamber proceedings were later released on bail. "Police have not decided whether to charge them," a police spokeswoman told Reuters.
Nearly 200 protesters from labour, Christian and Filipino groups demonstrated outside the building earlier, shouting slogans to denounce the debate inside.
"Hands off labour rights", "Shame on heavy-handed tactics against Hong Kong workers", "Say no to abolition of labour rights", they chanted, waving huge banners.
They then marched to Tung's office where they handed in a petition with 13,000 signatures opposing the move.

Tung said the laws at issue were questionable. "I think it is right for these laws to be frozen," he said. "We will study them carefully, consult the public and do what is right in the long-term interest of Hong Kong."

The rights enshrined in the suspended laws are in line with international labour conventions. Some legal experts say the suspension could spark a constitutional crisis as Hong Kong's constitution, the Basic Law, says it should apply standards set in those conventions.
